newsitem.title: FINLAND: KALLIOMAKI CAUTIOUSLY BULLISH ON JOBS CREATION.
newsitem.headline: KALLIOMAKI CAUTIOUSLY BULLISH ON JOBS CREATION.

text.p: Finnish Minister of Trade and Industry Antti Kalliomaki said on Thursday he saw joblessness declining at a fair pace, even if the government's goal of cutting unemployment in half was still some distance away.

"The decline in unemployment seems to be proceeding at a reasonable pace, though there is still a stretch to go to reach the goal of halving (unemployment)," Kalliomaki said in the prepared text of a speech to a trade union seminar.
Statistics Finland earlier on Thursday reported a fall in the jobless rate to 15.5 percent in December from 17.0 percent in November.
"To cut unemployment in half would require considerably faster growth than Finland, depite its good prospects, looks likely to achieve," Kalliomaki said.
Public employment support schemes could only be a temporary means to eliminate structural friction, Kalliomaki said.

"Although it is clear that public sector employment measures are needed and do produce results, they cannot be of more than marginal help in solving the current unemployment problem," he said. "In a market economy, permanent ... jobs can only be based on sustained demand because in the end wages paid for labour depend on the added value that can be achieved."
Small- and medium-sized service industry firms were particularly likely to hire new workers when demand was rising faster than existing staff could handle, Kalliomaki said.
"There must be a balance between the cost of labour and the economic result achieved by that labour if permanent jobs are to be created," he said.

Work must increasingly be done when -- and to the extent that -- it is needed, Kalliomaki said, adding that it was "simply impossible" in today's world to offer everyone jobs that were stable in terms of duration and amount of work.
Kalliomaki also said that performanced-based pay offered many people opportunities for better wage development.
